title: Video Call: The Only Permitted Exception
summary: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends zero screen time under the age of eighteen months, with one exception: video calls with relatives. The difference is that the call is a real, two-way social interaction (Grandma responds to the baby’s smile), not passive broadcasting. Even this should be short and with your presence, naming the person and encouraging the child to wave and coo. The screen here is a means of *silat al-rahim* (maintaining ties of kinship), not a means of entertainment—this is the balance that protects the child’s developing brain.
try_this: This week: Arrange a short video call (two minutes) with a beloved relative, and sit beside your child. Name the person, wave your child’s hand, and comment on the relative’s responses. Notice: Did your child interact (smile/coo) or remain a spectator?
reflection_prompts: What difference did you notice between your child’s attention during an interactive video call and leaving them in front of a broadcast video?
How can you make every moment of screen time (no matter how little) a moment of connection rather than a moment of silence?

review_defects.arabic: الشاشة هنا وسيلة علاقة لا وسيلة تسلية
review_defects.english: The screen here is a means of *silat al-rahim* (maintaining ties of kinship), not a means of entertainment
review_defects.why: The Arabic says 'وسيلة علاقة' (a means of relationship) without any Islamic terminology. The English adds the specific religious concept 'silat al-rahim' which is not present in the source, altering the meaning.
